title: RESEARCH GAP: Hamilton's first grocery/general store
note: NOT ESTABLISHED. No date or name has been verified by this project. Do not display until sourced; the Weekly Enterprise (Hamilton, 1890-1923) on Virginia Chronicle is the obvious place to look.

title: Leesburg Academy chartered
note: Chartered by the Virginia Assembly as a classical Latin grammar school for boys. Operated through the Civil War; its purpose-built building went up beside the Loudoun County Courthouse in 1844 and it moved to North Street in 1873.
source: Thomas Balch Library, 'Antebellum Leesburg (1814-1860)', Town of Leesburg

title: Washington DC becomes the federal capital
note: Government moves from Philadelphia

title: Virginia Literary Fund account established
note: Passed by the General Assembly in early 1810 (House 24 Jan, Senate 8 Feb); the account was set up in 1811. Funded from escheats, fines, forfeitures and land fees. THIS, NOT A SCHOOL SYSTEM, IS WHAT VIRGINIA HAD BEFORE 1870.
source: Library of Virginia, UncommonWealth, 'to the encouragement of learning: Virginia's Literary Fund'

title: War of 1812 begins
note: US declares war on Britain

title: Burning of Washington
note: British troops burn the Capitol and White House; Loudoun residents hear the news within days

title: Literary Fund act: $45,000 a year for educating the poor
note: The 1818 act set aside $15,000 a year for the University of Virginia and $45,000 for the education of the poor. County school commissioners ran the schooling; each locality drew about three and a half cents per child per day of actual attendance. Fund records at the Library of Virginia span 1794-1869, bulk 1811-1850.
source: Library of Virginia, UncommonWealth, 'to the encouragement of learning: Virginia's Literary Fund'

title: Genius of Liberty prints that teaching enslaved people to read is illegal
note: A letter signed 'Judex' in the Leesburg paper: 'the order of society must prevail over the notions of individuals.' NOTE: the Genius of Liberty is one of this project's own four sources - see loudoun_deaths.csv src_page 100-104.
source: Loudoun County Historical Society, 'Timeline of Important African American Events in Loudoun County' (loudounhistory.org)

title: Quaker schoolhouses at Purcellville and Lincoln reportedly taught Black and white children together
note: John Jay Janney's 1901 memoirs claim Black children on Quaker farms attended school with white children at the 'log schoolhouse in Purcellville' and the 'Goose Creek Friends' Schoolhouse' at today's Lincoln. A recollection written eighty years later and not independently corroborated.
source: Loudoun County Historical Society, 'Timeline of Important African American Events in Loudoun County' (loudounhistory.org)

title: C&O Canal and B&O Railroad both break ground
note: Both projects started the same day in Georgetown and Baltimore

title: Loudoun reportedly had 75 schools for 900 poor children
note: Open only 70 days a year. This is the Literary Fund system as it actually operated in this county. Race is not specified in the figure. Reported, not corroborated.
source: Loudoun County Historical Society, 'Timeline of Important African American Events in Loudoun County' (loudounhistory.org)

title: Virginia forbids Black people to assemble to read or write
note: Passed after Nat Turner's revolt (1831-32 session): enslaved and free Black people barred from assembling to read, write, or hear a Black preacher. Slaves of one master could still meet for prayer. A deliberate legal closing of the door that the Quaker schools had reportedly left ajar.
source: Loudoun County Historical Society, 'Timeline of Important African American Events in Loudoun County' (loudounhistory.org)

title: The Leesburg and Snickers Gap Turnpike Company opens the road through Hamilton
note: A toll road connecting Leesburg and Snickersville, opened 1831. It is the road through the middle of this town - today's Colonial Highway, SR 7 Business. Yardley Taylor's 1853 map labels it SNICKERS GAP TURNPIKE where it passes Hamilton P.O., corroborating the alignment. DO NOT CONFUSE with the Snicker's Gap Turnpike Company of 1810, a different company whose road ran Aldie-Mountville-Philomont-Airmont-Bluemont and is today's SR 734. That one had three toll gates over 17.5 miles per an 1851 state report; its gate locations are not established and it does not pass through Hamilton. NO SOURCE FOUND placing a tollgate at Harmony Church Road and Colonial Highway. A turnpike company operating from 1831 collected tolls at gates somewhere along this road, so a gate in or near the town is plausible - but plausible is not documented.
source: Hamilton, Virginia (Wikipedia) - secondary source, not yet corroborated against a primary record; Yardley Taylor, Map of Loudoun County, 1853, LC g3883l la001287; Snicker's Gap Turnpike (Wikipedia)

title: The Leesburg and Snickers Gap Turnpike is chartered
note: The road that becomes Colonial Highway through Hamilton, roughly forty years before the railroad.

title: Nat Turner's rebellion (Southampton County VA)
note: Prompted tighter slave codes across Virginia

title: Hamilton post office approved in Charles Bennett Hamilton's store
note: REFINED 26 Oct 2026, was 'exists by 1853'. A post office was approved in 1835 in the store founded by CHARLES BENNETT HAMILTON, and the town's name was recorded as Hamilton from that point - the place had been known as Harmony, after the estate built by Richard Tavenner and Ann Hatcher. HARD CORROBORATION: 'HAMILTON P.O.' is printed on Yardley Taylor's 1853 map beside E. J. HAMILTON and C. HAMILTON'S HEIRS, so the office certainly existed by 1853. THE 1835 DATE RESTS ON A SECONDARY SOURCE and is not yet corroborated against a postal or county record; the 1853 map evidence is the firm part.
source: Hamilton, Virginia (Wikipedia) - secondary source, not yet corroborated against a primary record; Yardley Taylor, Map of Loudoun County, 1853, LC g3883l la001287

title: Springdale Boarding School for Girls founded, Lincoln
note: Founded by the Quaker Samuel M. Janney in the Goose Creek community at today's Lincoln, roughly three miles from Hamilton. A girls' school in the Quaker tradition.

title: First telegraph message (Washington to Baltimore)
note: Morse's "What hath God wrought"

title: LOUDOUN COUNTY VOTES AGAINST ESTABLISHING PUBLIC SCHOOLS
note: Virginia let localities choose whether to establish public schools. Loudoun rejected the option, reportedly out of fear that the schools would have to admit free Black children. The county had the chance twenty-four years before 1870 and turned it down.
source: Loudoun County Historical Society, 'Timeline of Important African American Events in Loudoun County' (loudounhistory.org)

title: 29 of 49 surnames on the 1853 map are on headstones here
note: Of 49 householder surnames legible around Hamilton on Yardley Taylor's 1853 map, 29 also appear on stones in Lakeview, Harmony UMC or Pleasant Valley, covering 416 of the project's 2,732 people. Largest overlaps: Myers 43, Warner 41, Brown 36, Tavenner 35, Smith 30, Schooley 24, Beans 23, Gray 23, Thomas 20, Saunders 18. CAUTION: this is SURNAME overlap, not person identification - no map name has been matched to a person_id, and the map gives initials only.
source: Yardley Taylor, 'Map of Loudoun County, Virginia, from actual surveys', 1853 (Philadelphia: Thomas Reynolds & Robert Pearsall Smith, c.1854). Library of Congress, Geography and Map Division, G3883.L5G46 1854 .T3, digital id g3883l la001287

title: Taylor's 1853 map legend: 77 water powers employed in Loudoun County
note: THE MAP'S COMPLETE REFERENCE KEY, read at native resolution. Only four map abbreviations exist: P.O. Post Office; M.M. Merchant Mill; G.M. Grist Mill; S.M. Saw Mill. 'There are in the County 77 Water powers employed: 21 of them driving Merchant M[ills], 17 Merchant & Saw, 17 Grist & Saw Mills, 9 Grist Mills, 6 Saw Mills.' ARITHMETIC DISCREPANCY, verified by re-reading the figures at 1:1: 21+17+17+9+6 = 70, but Taylor's own total is 77. SEVEN WATER POWERS ARE EMPLOYED DRIVING SOMETHING HE DOES NOT ITEMISE - plausibly distilleries, fulling or carding mills, plaster mills, tanneries or forges, all common on Loudoun streams. NOT ESTABLISHED; do not fill the gap with a guess. HOUSES FOR PUBLIC WORSHIP BUILT: German Reformed 1, Lutheran 2, Episcopalian 3, Friends (Quakers) 4, Presbyterian 2, Baptist 6, Free 4, METHODIST 12, Methodist South 3 - 37 in the county. THERE IS NO TOLLGATE, TOLL HOUSE OR TURNPIKE-GATE SYMBOL ANYWHERE IN THE KEY. Taylor did not map tolls.
source: Yardley Taylor, Map of Loudoun County, Virginia, 1853 - the map's own reference key, lower-left of the sheet. LC Geography & Map, g3883l la001287. Read at 1:1, 26 Oct 2026.

title: 'M.M.H.' beside Hamilton on the 1853 map is a Methodist meeting house
note: RESOLVED from the map's own key: M.M.H. = Methodist Meeting House (the key lists 12 in the county). The symbol sits on the turnpike just northeast of HAMILTON P.O. Given its position it is very likely HARMONY METHODIST, on today's Harmony Church Road - but the map gives no church name and the identification is NOT established. IT IS NOT A TOLLBOOTH. Likewise the small star symbols further east along the turnpike, by W. Carr's heirs and near J. Thomas, carry mill abbreviations from the same key and are MILLS, not toll gates.
source: Yardley Taylor, Map of Loudoun County, Virginia, 1853 - the map's own reference key, lower-left of the sheet. LC Geography & Map, g3883l la001287. Read at 1:1, 26 Oct 2026.

title: John Snow traces cholera to the Broad Street pump
note: First strong evidence that a killer disease travels in water rather than air. Cholera appears in this dataset in 1853-54.

title: Dred Scott v. Sandford decided
note: The Court held that people of African descent whose ancestors were enslaved were not US citizens and could not sue in federal court, and that Congress had no authority to ban slavery in federal territories. Four years before the first death in this dataset's register period that could have been a Black decedent and was not recorded as one.

title: John Brown's raid on Harpers Ferry
note: About 25 miles from Hamilton; Loudoun militia called out

title: The railroad names Clarke's Gap after Addison H. Clarke
note: The gap through Catoctin Mountain west of Leesburg, elevation 643 ft. The Alexandria, Loudoun and Hampshire Railroad - predecessor of the W&OD - was routed through it in the 1860s and named its station, and so the gap, after a nearby landowner, ADDISON H. CLARKE. CORROBORATION IN THIS PROJECT'S OWN IMAGERY: 'A.H. Clarke' is printed on Yardley Taylor's 1853 map on the eastern slope of the Catoctin ridge, with 'J.W. Clarke' at the road crossing the gap itself - about a decade before the railroad borrowed the name. EARLIER NAME: the pass was Vestal's Gap, carrying Braddock's Road, the Alexandria-Winchester road, from the mid-18th century. Exact naming year NOT established; 1860 is a decade-level placeholder. No Addison Clarke is buried in the three cemeteries; the 12 Clark/Clarke interments are 8 Pleasant Valley, 2 Harmony, 2 Lakeview and no relationship to him is established. LOCAL TIE: Wesley Carruthers (HM0031, d.1904) was reported 'of Clarks Gap' in his death notice.
source: Clarke's Gap (Wikipedia); Yardley Taylor, Map of Loudoun County, 1853, LC g3883l la001287

title: Pasteur publishes the germ theory of fermentation
note: The intellectual turn that makes microbial causes of disease thinkable.

title: Virginia secession convention votes to secede
note: Loudoun County itself voted 1626 to 726 for secession on May 23 1861; Quaker and German precincts voted against

title: Homestead Act signed
note: Opens western land; one driver of out-migration from Loudoun farms.

title: Morrill Land-Grant Act signed
note: Creates the agricultural colleges; the beginning of scientific farming as a profession.

title: Lee's army fords the Potomac at White's Ford
note: Maryland Campaign passes through eastern Loudoun

title: Battles of Aldie, Middleburg and Upperville
note: Cavalry fighting across Loudoun during the Gettysburg campaign

title: The Burning Raid begins
note: Ordered by Grant (proposed to Sheridan 16 Aug 1864); Sheridan issued the operational order 27 Nov to Maj. Gen. Wesley Merritt. Merritt's 1st Cavalry Division burned barns and mills and drove off livestock across western Loudoun and northern Fauquier, between the Blue Ridge and the Bull Run and Catoctin mountains. Dwellings were not to be burned. THE 2ND BRIGADE PASSED THROUGH HAMILTON ON 30 NOVEMBER 1864, heading north through Waterford along Catoctin Creek. Reserve Brigade's own report: 230 barns, 8 mills and 1 distillery burned, 10,000 tons of hay and 25,000 bushels of grain destroyed. Merritt's preliminary report: 5,000-6,000 cattle, 3,000-4,000 sheep, 500-700 horses driven off, c.1,000 hogs slaughtered. Places named as hit: Upperville, Middleburg, Philomont, Snickersville, Purcellville, Round Hill, Hillsboro, Lincoln, Lovettsville, Taylorstown. Ends 2 Dec.
source: Loudoun Museum / loudounhistory.org, "Loudoun County Burning Raid and John S. Mosby"

title: Emancipation remakes Loudoun labour
note: In 1860 Loudoun held 5,501 enslaved and 1,251 free Black people, 31 percent of the county. The agricultural labour system is rebuilt from here. See context_demography.csv.

title: Freedmen's Bureau opens headquarters at Leesburg and Middleburg
note: Tasked with educating freed people. In May 1865 the diarist Catherine Broun recorded Black people carrying school books and Union soldiers teaching them.
source: Loudoun County Historical Society, 'Timeline of Important African American Events in Loudoun County' (loudounhistory.org)

title: 13th Amendment ratified; slavery abolished
note: Passed by Congress 31 Jan 1865. The legal end of slavery, two years after the Emancipation Proclamation and the real boundary for this dataset: every racial marking in the project falls after this date.

title: Black elementary schools built at Lincoln and Waterford
note: Built with help from Quakers, Baptists and the Freedmen's Bureau. The Lincoln school was known as 'Janney's School'. Earlier, late 1865 or January 1866, the Bureau had established a school at Middleburg and another across the road from present Asbury Methodist Church near Hillsboro.
source: Loudoun County Historical Society, 'Timeline of Important African American Events in Loudoun County' (loudounhistory.org)

title: Two Freedmen's Bureau schools operating in Leesburg
note: 'The African School', probably at the Northern Methodist Church, and 'Bailey's School' on South King Street. The Washingtonian of 22 June 1866 reported Reverend William L. Robey teaching freed boys and girls at the African School.
source: Loudoun County Historical Society, 'Timeline of Important African American Events in Loudoun County' (loudounhistory.org)

title: Waterford School built
note: Funded by the Freedmen's Bureau and Philadelphia Friends, 'a school house for colored children and for church purposes'. Black trustees had bought the land in July 1866. It served about ninety years.
source: Loudoun County Historical Society, 'Timeline of Important African American Events in Loudoun County' (loudounhistory.org)

title: Lister introduces antiseptic surgery
note: Carbolic acid on wounds; surgical mortality falls sharply.

title: Willisville school built for $150; Freedmen's Bureau closes its Loudoun offices
note: 'To be used for the education of the colored youth of Willisville and for church purposes on Sabbath Day' - the first public school for Black children in southwest Loudoun. The Bureau closed its Loudoun offices the same year.
source: Loudoun County Historical Society, 'Timeline of Important African American Events in Loudoun County' (loudounhistory.org)

title: The railroad reaches Hamilton
note: A steam railroad from Alexandria had reached Hamilton by 1868, along what became the Washington and Old Dominion. CORRECTS the 1870 date flagged as unsourced in the film script (shots 1.22-1.24). Secondary source; worth corroborating against a railroad or county record before it is narrated.
source: Hamilton, Virginia (Wikipedia) - secondary source, not yet corroborated against a primary record

title: 14th Amendment ratified
note: Passed by Congress 13 Jun 1866; a State Department certificate of 28 Jul 1868 declared ratification by 28 of 37 states. Citizenship and equal protection.

title: The HARMONY school for Black children opens at Brownsville, just east of Hamilton
note: By March 1869 seven schools educated Black children in Loudoun County: near Hillsboro, and at Leesburg, Lincoln, Middleburg, Waterford, Willisville, and 'Harmony'. LOCATION RESOLVED: the school stood at Brownsville (also called Swampoodle), a community just east of Hamilton, on property belonging to WILLIAM H. AND MARION P. BROWN, white Quakers who let the Freedmen's Bureau open it on their land just after the war. It had 64 STUDENTS IN 1870, taught by a Black teacher, ELLIS S. PORTER. Hamilton was named Harmony until 1875, which is where the school's name comes from. This is the earliest documented school for Black children in this immediate area - 53 years before Pleasant Valley Cemetery was established and 72 years before Loudoun had a Black high school. An earlier source gave the location as 'either Hamilton or nearby Brownsville'; the communities record is more specific and names the family, the teacher and the enrolment.
source: Loudoun County Historical Society, 'African American Communities' and 'Timeline of Important African American Events in Loudoun County' (loudounhistory.org)

title: Virginia's readmission requires a segregated public school system
note: The Underwood Convention of 1867-68, which Snickersville physician George Emory Plaster attended for Loudoun, had provided for statewide public education. Freedmen's Bureau schools of the 1860s became the public schools for Black children. Loudoun's first school superintendent, Donald Wildman, reported to the state in 1872 on Black families' willingness to sacrifice for education.
source: Loudoun County Historical Society, 'Timeline of Important African American Events in Loudoun County' (loudounhistory.org)

title: Montclair, New Jersey begins recruiting Loudoun labour
note: A Montclair businessman brought Loudoun African Americans north to work as house servants as early as 1870. This seeded the chain migration that carried Loudoun families to Montclair for the next eighty years - probably numbering in the hundreds. Montclair's Black population grew from about 2,500 in 1910 to 6,300 in 1930.

title: Virginia readmitted to the Union
note: January 26 1870

title: 15th Amendment ratified
note: Passed by Congress 26 Feb 1869. The right to vote regardless of race, which Virginia dismantled in practice 32 years later.

title: Washington and Ohio Railroad reaches Hamilton
note: The line later became the W&OD; station at Hamilton opened the town to summer boarders and Washington trade [FLAGGED 24 Oct 2026: 1874 is unsourced and looks too late. A Clarke County deed book of 1868-1871 reckons the line "from Alexandria to Hamilton Station" and describes construction running westward FROM Hamilton; every Loudoun record naming "Hamilton Station" falls 1870-1875. Verify.]

title: Town of Hamilton incorporated
note: Previously Harmony / Harmony Village [FLAGGED 24 Oct 2026: incorporation year unsourced; checked sources give an 1835 post office and no incorporation date. Verify.]

title: Koch proves a bacterium causes anthrax
note: Germ theory moves from hypothesis to demonstration.

title: Mt. Zion Methodist Church founded (Hamilton)
note: The church of Hamilton's Black community on "the Hill", north of town. Still active.

title: Koch identifies the tubercle bacillus
note: The cause of CONSUMPTION is finally known. Consumption is by far the commonest cause of death in this dataset: 183 entries, spanning 1819 to 1890. Knowing the cause did not yet mean being able to treat it - that waits until 1944.

title: Klebs and Loeffler identify the diphtheria bacillus
note: Diphtheria killed Willie N. Taylor at Lakeview in 1866 and three Carter children in six days of May 1865. 18 diphtheria deaths are recorded here, all 1864-66.

title: Pasteur first uses the rabies vaccine
Brownsville (Harmony) School opens as a public school
note: Opened 1887 to serve Black students from the Jefferson and Mt. Gilead school districts. DISTINCT FROM THE 1869 FREEDMEN'S BUREAU SCHOOL at the same community: the Bureau school is attested by March 1869 on the Browns' land, the county's GIS record dates this school building to 1887, in the public-school era. Whether they share a site or a lineage is NOT established and must not be asserted.
source: Loudoun County GIS, COL/Historic MapServer — layer 0 Historic Communities, layer 3 Cemetery (logis.loudoun.gov)

title: Scarlet fever in Hamilton; typhoid case reported
note: The town's own paper: '... is at this time lying very low with typhoid fever. Some mild cases of scarlet fever in town.' The earliest local epidemic report recovered for Hamilton itself.

title: Second Mount Olive Baptist Church founded (Brownsville)
note: Serving Brownsville/Swampoodle, just east of Hamilton. Built on land DONATED BY NANCY MURRAY. Still active. The same community that hosted the Harmony Freedmen's Bureau school in 1869.

title: Diphtheria antitoxin enters wide use
note: THE FIRST DISEASE IN THIS DATASET TO BECOME TREATABLE. Child mortality from diphtheria falls steeply from here.

title: Widal test allows typhoid to be diagnosed
note: 69 typhoid deaths are recorded here, 1853-1882, including the 1866 wave that killed Annie Arabella Everhart.

title: Plessy v. Ferguson decided
note: Separate-but-equal held constitutional. Upheld racial segregation for roughly fifty years.
source: Library of Congress, Today in History (18 May)

title: Rural Free Delivery begins
note: Mail to the farm gate; the country store loses its role as the post office.

title: Virginia constitutional convention convenes, Richmond
note: Met in two sessions, 12 Jun 1901 to 26 Jun 1902, for the express purpose of disfranchising Black voters.

title: Mail-order catalogue retailing reaches rural Virginia at scale
Virginia Constitution of 1902 completed
note: Suffrage rules applied to elections from 1902 to 1904: an 'understanding clause' requiring applicants to read and explain any section of the constitution, a one-dollar property-tax requirement, unassisted application in the applicant's own handwriting, and an exemption for men who served, or whose fathers served, in US or Confederate forces.

title: Wright brothers fly at Kitty Hawk
Virginia poll tax takes effect; Black registration collapses
note: Enabling legislation added a poll tax of $1.50 for each of the three preceding years. Registered Black voters in Virginia fell from about 147,000 in 1900 to about 21,000 in 1904, and fewer than half of those qualified. Black votes in the 1904 presidential election fell about 90 percent.

title: Chlorination of a US public water supply begins (Jersey City)
note: Waterborne typhoid and dysentery begin their collapse. Dysentery is the second commonest cause in this dataset: 141 entries, every one between 1853 and 1866.

title: Ford Model T introduced
note: Already in this dataset under the national layer; repeated here because of what it does to rural trade patterns.

title: Milk pasteurisation spreads through US cities
note: Cuts infant diarrhoeal death and bovine tuberculosis.

title: World War I begins in Europe
United States enters World War I
Influenza pandemic peaks in Virginia
note: Several Lakeview stones date from Oct-Nov 1918

title: The US census records a majority-urban nation for the first time
note: The long drain from farm to town, visible in Loudoun as elsewhere.

title: BCG vaccine first given to a human
Pleasant Valley Cemetery established
note: One of Loudoun's largest African American cemeteries, on Harmony Church Road. It is the SECOND location of this burial ground; the first was at Harmony UMC. 368 burials in this dataset, effectively all after 1922.

title: LOUDOUN COUNTY HEALTH UNIT OPERATING - organised public health arrives
note: 'The Medical Director has already begun his campaign against Diphtheria. The Sanitary Officer has already begun sanitating the schools.' Within ten weeks: Schick testing at Aldie (27 Apr), prevention work in five schools with many children found susceptible (25 May), public immunisation offered to Leesburg parents (15 Jun), and four typhoid cases COUNTED and reported county-wide (29 Jun). THIS IS WHERE BACTERIOLOGY STOPS BEING NATIONAL NEWS AND BECOMES SOMETHING HAPPENING TO CHILDREN IN THIS COUNTY. See hamilton_health_news.csv.

title: Virginia Racial Integrity Act signed
note: Signed by Gov. E. Lee Trinkle. Defined a white person as one with 'no trace whatsoever of any blood other than Caucasian', banned interracial marriage, required birth and marriage records to note race, and placed the burden of proof on the individual. Proposed by the Anglo-Saxon Clubs of America, founded 1922 by Walter A. Plecker, Ernest S. Cox and John Powell; Plecker, as state registrar, enforced a stricter 'trace of negro blood' standard in practice. The marriage ban stood until Loving v. Virginia, 12 Jun 1967. The General Assembly denounced the act and eugenics in 2001.

title: Brownsville (Harmony) School closes to students
note: Converted into a private residence. The Black school serving Hamilton's eastern community operated roughly 38 years.
source: Loudoun County GIS, COL/Historic MapServer — layer 0 Historic Communities, layer 3 Cemetery (logis.loudoun.gov)

title: Virginia Public Assemblages Act becomes law
note: Required the separation of white and colored persons at public halls, theatres and other public gatherings. Introduced by George Alvin Massenburg 20 Jan 1926; House 63-3, Senate 30-5; Gov. Harry F. Byrd Sr. let it become law without his signature. Hampton Institute stopped opening its events to the public rather than comply.

title: Fleming observes penicillin
note: Observation only; a usable drug is still fifteen years away.

title: Virginia redefines 'colored' to include any 'negro blood'
note: Signed by Gov. John Garland Pollard. Recognised as tribal Indians only those living on the state's two reservations with at least one-fourth Indian blood; all other Virginia Indians were reclassified 'colored'. Opposed by Pamunkey chief George Major Cook.

title: Franklin Roosevelt inaugurated; New Deal begins
Sulfonamides reach the market
note: The first antibacterial drugs that actually work. Pneumonia, scarlet fever, puerperal fever and many wound infections become survivable. 70 pneumonia deaths are recorded here.

title: Rural Electrification Administration created
note: Electricity reaches Loudoun farms over the following decade. One of the largest single changes to rural daily life in this entire timeline.

title: Fair Labor Standards Act
note: Minimum wage, the 44-hour week, and limits on child labour.

title: Douglass High School opens, Leesburg
note: First high school for African American students in Loudoun County. Before 1941 Black secondary students had no county high school; the only option was the upper level of the Loudoun County Training School.
source: Douglass High School (Leesburg, VA) - Wikipedia, cross-checked LCPS Douglass Community Center history page

title: Streptomycin: the first effective treatment for tuberculosis
note: CONSUMPTION BECOMES CURABLE, 62 years after Koch found its cause and more than a century after it began filling these graves.

title: Post-war farm mechanisation accelerates
note: Tractors displace horses and hired hands; farm employment falls steeply.

title: Brown v. Board of Education decided
note: Segregation in public schools declared unconstitutional. Brown II, 31 May 1955, ordered desegregation 'with all deliberate speed'. Loudoun County did not desegregate for another fourteen years.

title: Salk polio vaccine declared safe and effective
Senator Harry F. Byrd Sr. calls for Massive Resistance
note: The public launch of Virginia's organised refusal to comply with Brown.

title: Federal-Aid Highway Act
note: The interstate system; the beginning of Loudoun as commuter country.

title: Governor Stanley announces the Stanley Plan
note: The Massive Resistance legislative package, passed by the General Assembly in special session that August.

title: Virginia begins closing schools rather than desegregate
note: Warren County High School (Front Royal) closed 15 Sep 1958; Lane High School and Venable Elementary (Charlottesville) 19 Sep; white secondary schools in Norfolk 27 Sep. Gov. Almond had stripped superintendents of authority to desegregate on 4 Sep.

title: Massive Resistance ruled unconstitutional
note: The federal district court and the Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals both ruled the school closings unconstitutional on the same day. Seventeen Black students enrolled in white schools in Norfolk and four in Arlington on 2 Feb 1959. In April the General Assembly replaced Massive Resistance with the Perrow Plan's limited 'freedom of choice'.

title: Dulles International Airport opens
note: Eastern Loudoun begins its shift from agriculture to suburb.

title: Measles vaccine licensed
note: 10 measles deaths are recorded here, including Francis E. Hoskinson at Harmony in 1858.

title: 24th Amendment ratified
note: Barred denying a vote in federal elections for failure to pay a poll tax.

title: Civil Rights Act signed
note: Signed 2 Jul 1964. Did not by itself desegregate Loudoun's schools; that waited on Green in 1968.

title: Voting Rights Act signed
note: Guaranteed that no person would be denied the vote on grounds of race or colour. Sixty-three years after Virginia's 1902 constitution, and the end of the disfranchisement era in this timeline.

title: Loudoun County public schools desegregated
note: Fourteen years after Brown v. Board. Douglass High School became a middle school.

title: Green v. New Kent County strikes down 'freedom of choice'
note: Large-scale school desegregation begins across Virginia. THIS IS WHY LOUDOUN DESEGREGATED IN 1968 - the county did not act on its own.

title: Last W&OD train runs
note: The railroad that built Hamilton is abandoned; the corridor becomes the W&OD Trail

title: Part of Harmony UMC's burial ground for its enslaved congregants is paved for a parking lot
note: Witnesses saw the work and were not told whether remains had been removed. Surviving stones were later consolidated into one communal marker. Decade approximate.

title: Graves at Harmony UMC believed to be historically African American were disturbed by parking-lot construction
note: LOUDOUN COUNTY'S OWN CEMETERY RECORD (PCEM-1998-0072) states: 'Graves believed to be historically African-American were disturbed during construction of a parking lot pre-2000.' THIS IS DOCUMENTARY CORROBORATION, FROM COUNTY GOVERNMENT, OF THE HAMILTON LEGEND ABOUT THE MOVED OR LOST STONES AT HARMONY METHODIST. AERIAL SURVEY 26 Oct 2026 (see harmony_aerial_survey.csv) NARROWS THE DATE: the lot is ABSENT in 1957, 1980 and 1990, INDETERMINATE in 1994, and clearly PRESENT with painted striping in 2002. There is no frame between 1994 and 2002. Combined with the county's 'pre-2000', the lot was built BETWEEN 1994 AND 2000, and certainly after 1990. The date on this row (2000) remains an UPPER BOUND, not the event date. NOT ESTABLISHED: which pavement overlaps the historic burial ground, how many graves, whose, or where they went. The aerial reading is interpretation of imagery, not a document.
source: Loudoun County GIS, COL/Historic MapServer — layer 0 Historic Communities, layer 3 Cemetery (logis.loudoun.gov)
